questions.stem: In Snowflake account replication, what is a replicated object in a target account called?

options.text: A secondary object
A primary object
A source object
A shadow object

explanation.correct: Replicated objects in a target account are called secondary objects; they are replicas of the primary objects in the source account.

distractors.B: Primary objects live in the source account, not the target account.
distractors.C: The source is the account being replicated from, not the replicated object.
distractors.D: Snowflake does not use the term 'shadow object' for replicas.

questions.stem: Which TWO replication capabilities are available on ALL Snowflake editions (including Standard)? (Select TWO)

options.text: Database replication
Share replication
Failover groups
Tri-Secret Secure data protection
Dataset replication

explanation.correct: Database replication and share replication are available on all editions including Standard. Replication Group is also available on all editions.

distractors.C: Failover groups require Business Critical Edition or higher.
distractors.D: Tri-Secret Secure data protection requires Business Critical Edition or higher.
distractors.E: Dataset replication requires Business Critical Edition or higher.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a replication group and a failover group?

options.text: A replication group can fail over; a failover group is read-only only
They are identical terms with no functional difference
A replication group works across regions; a failover group only works within a region
A failover group is a replication group that can also fail over (be promoted to primary for read-write access)

explanation.correct: A failover group is a replication group that can also fail over. Its secondary provides read-only access until promoted to primary, which enables read-write access.

distractors.A: This is reversed: the failover group is the one that can fail over.
distractors.B: They differ: only a failover group supports promotion/failover.
distractors.C: Both support cross-region replication; the distinction is failover capability, not region scope.

questions.stem: Which THREE features require Business Critical Edition (or higher) according to the replication feature/edition matrix? (Select THREE)

options.text: Database replication
Failover Group
Share replication
Account object (other than database and share) replication
Replication Group
Data protected with Tri-Secret Secure

explanation.correct: Failover Group, account object (non-database/share) replication, and Tri-Secret Secure data protection all require Business Critical Edition or higher.

distractors.A: Database replication is available on all editions including Standard.
distractors.C: Share replication is available on all editions including Standard.
distractors.E: Replication Group is available on all editions including Standard.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about Snowflake Client Redirect are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: The primary and secondary connections can be in the same region
It is implemented through a Snowflake connection object storing a connection URL
The connection URL specifies the exact account you connect to
It requires Business Critical Edition (or higher)
It is available on all Snowflake editions

explanation.correct: Client Redirect is implemented via a connection object that stores a secure connection URL, and it requires Business Critical Edition or higher.

distractors.A: The accounts storing primary and secondary connections must be in different regions.
distractors.C: The connection URL does NOT specify the account; the primary connection determines the target account.
distractors.E: It is not available on all editions; it needs Business Critical or higher.

questions.scenario: An administrator signs into a target account and wants to promote a secondary failover group to become the primary during a disaster.
questions.stem: Which SQL command performs this promotion?

options.text: ALTER FAILOVER GROUP myfg REFRESH
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP myfg PRIMARY
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP myfg SET PRIMARY = TRUE
PROMOTE FAILOVER GROUP myfg

explanation.correct: ALTER FAILOVER GROUP <name> PRIMARY promotes a secondary failover group to serve as the primary, executed on the target account by a role with the FAILOVER privilege.

distractors.A: REFRESH synchronizes the secondary with the primary; it does not promote it.
distractors.C: This is not valid syntax for promoting a failover group.
distractors.D: PROMOTE FAILOVER GROUP is not a valid Snowflake command.

questions.scenario: During a partial outage in the source region, an administrator tries to promote a secondary failover group but it is currently being refreshed by a replication operation.
questions.stem: What does Snowflake do?

options.text: It prevents failover to ensure data integrity while a refresh is in progress
It immediately cancels the refresh and promotes the group
It silently promotes the group and discards the refresh
It duplicates the group into two primaries

explanation.correct: To ensure data integrity, Snowflake prevents failover if a refresh operation is in progress; you cannot promote a secondary while it is being refreshed.

distractors.B: Snowflake does not automatically cancel the refresh to force promotion in this SQL path.
distractors.C: It does not silently promote and discard; it blocks the failover.
distractors.D: There is never more than one primary; two primaries would break consistency.

questions.scenario: A company replicates a database from a Snowflake account in one region to a secondary account in a different region on the same cloud platform.
questions.stem: How are data transfer costs applied?

options.text: No data transfer costs apply because it is the same cloud platform
Data egress costs apply for transferring data out of the source region
Data ingress costs apply at the target account
Costs apply only if the accounts are in different organizations

explanation.correct: Snowflake charges a per-byte egress fee when data moves to a different region on the same cloud platform (or to a different cloud). Replication across regions incurs data transfer costs.

distractors.A: Same cloud platform but different region still incurs egress charges; only same-region transfers are free.
distractors.C: Snowflake does not charge data ingress fees.
distractors.D: Cost depends on region/cloud boundaries, not organization membership.

questions.scenario: A team is auditing which activities could incur Snowflake data transfer (egress) costs.
questions.stem: Which THREE actions can incur data transfer costs when crossing a region or cloud boundary? (Select THREE)

options.text: Querying data within the same region
Retrieving query results across regions via a client driver
Replicating databases to a secondary account in another region
Unloading data with COPY INTO <location> to storage in a different region
Cross-Cloud Auto-Fulfillment of listings to consumers in other cloud regions
Loading data into a table within the same region

explanation.correct: Replication across regions, unloading data to a different region, and Cross-Cloud Auto-Fulfillment all incur data transfer costs when crossing region/cloud boundaries.

distractors.A: Data transfers within the same region are free.
distractors.B: Snowflake does not apply egress charges when a client/driver retrieves query results across regions or clouds.
distractors.F: Snowflake does not charge data ingress fees for loading data.

questions.scenario: An application connects to Snowflake using a connection URL. An outage hits the region hosting the primary connection.
questions.stem: How does an administrator restore connectivity WITHOUT changing the application's connection settings?

options.text: Edit the application's config to point at the secondary account's URL
Promote a secondary connection in another region to primary using ALTER CONNECTION myconnection PRIMARY
Drop the primary connection and recreate it in the new region
Switch the application to a direct account locator URL

explanation.correct: The administrator promotes a secondary connection in a different region to primary with ALTER CONNECTION <name> PRIMARY; clients keep using the same connection URL, which now resolves to the promoted account.

distractors.A: The whole point of Client Redirect is that you do NOT change the application's connection settings.
distractors.C: Dropping and recreating the connection is unnecessary and would change the URL.
distractors.D: Switching to a direct account locator changes the application's connection settings, defeating Client Redirect.

questions.scenario: An organization wants to replicate objects between a Snowflake commercial region and a Snowflake government region (different region groups).
questions.stem: What is required to enable this cross-region-group replication?

options.text: Nothing; all regions replicate freely by default
They must contact Snowflake Support to enable it
They must downgrade both accounts to Standard Edition
Cross-region-group replication is impossible under any circumstances

explanation.correct: Customers can replicate across regions within a region group by default; to replicate between different region groups (e.g., commercial to government or VPS), they must contact Snowflake Support.

distractors.A: Free replication applies within a region group, not across different region groups.
distractors.C: Edition downgrade is unrelated and would remove needed features.
distractors.D: It is possible but requires contacting Snowflake Support.

questions.scenario: An engineer sets up Client Redirect for two accounts (myaccount1 as source, myaccount2 as target) in the same organization but different regions.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about creating the connections are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: The primary connection is created on the target account
Failover is enabled with GRANT FAILOVER ON CONNECTION
The secondary connection must have the same name as the primary connection
The secondary is created with CREATE CONNECTION myconnection AS REPLICA OF myorg.myaccount1.myconnection
The connection name must differ between primary and secondary

explanation.correct: The secondary connection must share the same name as the primary, and it is created with CREATE CONNECTION <name> AS REPLICA OF <org.account.connection>.

distractors.A: The primary connection is created on the source account, not the target.
distractors.B: Failover is enabled with ALTER CONNECTION ... ENABLE FAILOVER TO ACCOUNTS, not a GRANT statement.
distractors.E: The names must match, not differ.

questions.stem: What is the format of a Client Redirect connection URL hostname?

options.text: account_locator.region.snowflakecomputing.com
organization_name-connection_name.snowflakecomputing.com
connection_name.organization_name.snowflake.net
account_name-region.snowflakecomputing.com

explanation.correct: The connection URL hostname is composed of the organization name and connection object name: organization_name-connection_name.snowflakecomputing.com.

distractors.A: This resembles a standard account locator URL, not a Client Redirect connection URL.
distractors.C: The domain and ordering are incorrect for a connection URL.
distractors.D: The connection URL uses the connection name, not the account name and region.

questions.scenario: A team wants to replicate some databases more frequently than others within the same disaster-recovery setup.
questions.stem: How can they achieve differing refresh frequencies?

options.text: Divide the replicated objects across multiple failover groups
Use a single failover group with per-object schedules
Replication frequency cannot be customized per object
Create one failover group per region only

explanation.correct: You can optionally divide replicated objects across multiple failover groups, for example if some databases should be replicated more frequently than others.

distractors.B: Refresh schedules are set per failover group, not per object within a single group.
distractors.C: It can be customized by splitting objects into multiple groups with different schedules.
distractors.D: Grouping by region alone does not control refresh frequency per database.

questions.scenario: An administrator is performing a bulk failover in Snowsight and some refresh operations for the selected failover groups are still in progress.
questions.stem: Which TWO options does Snowsight offer to handle the in-progress refreshes? (Select TWO)

options.text: Automatically roll back all failover groups
Wait for the refreshes to complete (the default action)
Merge the primary and secondary into a single account
Permanently disable replication for the account
Cancel refreshes and force failover

explanation.correct: Snowsight defaults to waiting for refreshes to complete, or you can select 'Cancel refreshes and force failover' (advanced option) to proceed immediately, cleaning up any inconsistencies afterward.

distractors.A: Snowsight does not offer an automatic rollback of all groups as a refresh-handling option.
distractors.C: Merging accounts is not a failover option.
distractors.D: Disabling replication is not offered as a way to handle in-progress refreshes.

questions.scenario: After failover, the objects in a promoted failover group become writable on the newly promoted account.
questions.stem: What happens to those same objects on the account that was formerly the primary?

options.text: They remain writable on both accounts simultaneously
They are automatically dropped from the former primary
They are converted to transient objects
They become read-only on the former primary (now a secondary account)

explanation.correct: After failover, objects become writable on the newly promoted primary and become read-only on the account that formerly was the primary and is now a secondary account.

distractors.A: Only one account can hold the writable primary; the former primary becomes read-only.
distractors.B: Objects are not dropped from the former primary; they become read-only replicas.
distractors.C: Failover does not convert objects to transient objects.

questions.scenario: A finance team reviews whether Snowflake or the cloud provider charges for data movement into their Snowflake account.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about ingress and egress are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Snowflake charges ingress fees for all loaded data
Data transfers within the same region are charged per byte by Snowflake
Snowflake charges egress on query results retrieved across regions by a driver
Snowflake does not charge data ingress fees
A cloud storage provider might charge its own egress fee to move data to your Snowflake account

explanation.correct: Snowflake does not charge data ingress fees, but a cloud storage provider might charge its own egress fee to transfer data from its network to where your Snowflake account is hosted.

distractors.A: Snowflake does not charge ingress fees.
distractors.B: Data transfers within the same region are free.
distractors.C: Snowflake does not apply egress charges when a client/driver retrieves query results across regions or clouds.

questions.scenario: A prerequisite step in setting up disaster recovery is bringing the latest updates from the primary objects to each secondary account.
questions.stem: What is this synchronization operation called?

options.text: Failover
Failback
Promotion
Refresh

explanation.correct: Refresh synchronizes each replica (secondary failover group) with the latest updates to the objects in the primary failover group. An initial refresh plus a regular schedule keeps secondaries current.

distractors.A: Failover promotes a secondary to primary; it is not the sync operation.
distractors.B: Failback returns the primary role to the original source after an outage.
distractors.C: Promotion is the failover act, not the periodic synchronization.

questions.scenario: A data platform lead is planning a business-continuity architecture and listing the prerequisites for account failover.
questions.stem: Which THREE are prerequisites for failing over replicated account objects? (Select THREE)

options.text: Convert all databases to transient databases
Disable Time Travel on the source account
Enable replication in a set of accounts within the same organization across multiple regions
Create a primary failover group defining which objects to replicate and the target accounts
Create at least one secondary failover group in one or more secondary accounts
Move all accounts into a single region

explanation.correct: Prerequisites include enabling replication across accounts in the same organization/multiple regions, creating a primary failover group, and creating at least one secondary failover group (then refreshing it).

distractors.A: Converting databases to transient is not a failover prerequisite and would remove Fail-safe protection.
distractors.B: Disabling Time Travel is not required for failover.
distractors.F: Failover requires accounts in DIFFERENT regions, not a single region.

questions.scenario: An administrator promotes a target account to serve as the source account using Snowsight and wants the most consistent, reliable failover experience.
questions.stem: What does Snowflake recommend for this operation?

options.text: Fail over each group individually, one at a time, always
Select all applicable failover groups and connections and promote them together (a bulk failover)
Promote only connections and leave failover groups untouched
Delete the primary account before promoting the target

explanation.correct: For the most consistent and reliable failover, Snowflake recommends selecting all applicable failover groups and connections and promoting them all at the same time — a bulk failover.

distractors.A: One-at-a-time promotion is a fallback (e.g., to retry a failed group), not the recommended default for a full account failover.
distractors.C: Promoting only connections without failover groups would leave objects on the old primary.
distractors.D: Deleting the primary account is never part of the failover procedure.
